prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction and experimental discovery of flat bands, correlated insulators and superconductivity in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is a clear verified discovery in a stable two-dimensional material: a continuum-model prediction of flat bands at a specific twist angle (Bistritzer and MacDonald, 2011) was followed by the observation of gate-tunable correlated insulators and superconductivity (Jarillo-Herrero and collaborators, 2018), with STM evidence of flat bands and van Hove singularities from Andrei's group. Experiment and theory reinforce each other, and the main phenomena have since been reproduced by many independent groups using transport, STM and spectroscopy. It created a new platform, moire quantum materials, in which interaction-driven phases are tuned by a gate and an angle, and it is a good example of experiment surprising theory in a 2D crystal. Eight years is short, but the field's size and the breadth of independent confirmation make the core discovery robust enough to recognise.
statement.case_against: The nature of the superconducting pairing and of the correlated states is still unsettled, so the prize would honour a discovery whose interpretation is open; the field is young compared with topological insulators or optical clocks. Credit is also delicate: the three-name limit forces a choice among Bistritzer, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Andrei, and dropping Bistritzer (the first author of the prediction) is a real cost. Reproducibility is good for the phenomena but sample-to-sample variation in twist-angle disorder remains a worry.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks topological insulators first as a simple, general organising principle (a bulk invariant dictating protected boundary states) with long and independent experimental confirmation, and argues that recognition is arguably overdue.
responses.response: I agree on the confirmation record and on the generality of the idea, and I ranked B024 second myself; first-principles theory has also predicted topological materials that were then verified. My reservation is that the field was already partly recognised through the 2016 topological-phase prize and that the credit for B024 is awkward (Mele and Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang each have a strong claim, and a four-name list cannot be reduced to three without an obvious injustice). Twisted bilayer graphene offers a cleaner theory-plus-experiment attribution. I would not stand in the way of B024 if the committee finds a defensible trio.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first: the magic-wavelength idea plus record 1e-18 uncertainty is a new way of measuring time, mature and reproduced across many institutes, with a clean two-name credit (Katori and Ye).
responses.response: The credit is the cleanest on the shortlist and the independent confirmation across institutes is excellent, and I accept that as a serious competing case. As a condensed-matter physicist I defer on how much new physics lies beyond instrument improvement over the 2005 comb prize; the discovery content looks to me more like a precision-measurement milestone than a new state of matter or quantum behaviour. I would want to hear whether the atomic-physics colleagues see a distinct physical discovery, such as many-body effects in the lattice, rather than excellent engineering.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the IceCube high-energy neutrino discovery (Halzen alone) first, as a new observational window confirmed by multi-wavelength follow-up, with a single clean name credit.
responses.response: This is outside my area and I defer on the astrophysics. My concern is attribution rather than science: IceCube was a very large collaboration with AMANDA and DUMAND predecessors, and a single-laureate prize may read as crediting an instrument leader for a collective result. The source identification is also still incomplete beyond the diffuse flux, so maturity is the part I would like Pearce and Danielsson to press.

responses.point: Lindroth places clocks first and quantum simulation with ultracold atoms in optical lattices second, valuing simple physical tricks that open new regimes, and calls the lattice work timely and possibly overdue.
responses.response: I agree that ultracold-atom lattice simulation of the Hubbard model is mature and has been confirmed by dozens of groups. My qualification is that the five-name credit is hard to cut to three without leaving out Zoller's or Esslinger's decisive contributions, and the 2001 BEC and 2012 prizes overlap neighbouring ground. In my area the Hubbard model is also tackled by DMFT and DFT-based methods, so the simulation claim should be assessed against what calculations already gave.

uncertainties: Whether the superconducting pairing mechanism in twisted bilayer graphene needs to be settled before the committee considers the discovery mature enough.
How to allocate the three places among Bistritzer, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Andrei, and whether Andrei's early STM evidence is decisive enough to displace Bistritzer.
Whether a defensible three-person split of the topological insulator credit (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Hasan, with Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang outside the list) exists.
Whether optical lattice clocks carry a distinct physical discovery beyond precision instrumentation, which I cannot judge well from solid-state physics.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. I have no recorded personal or institutional connection to the credited candidates for B013, B024 or B001; my Los Alamos and Uppsala ties and my co-authors are not linked to them in the provided profile.
